column3: Presents worship and prostration without arrogance as the direct opposite of the focus response.
Begins the surrounding tribunal that gathers the wrongdoers and what they worshipped besides God.
Their acknowledgement that all belongs to God exposes the gap between correct confession and faithful response.
Those reminded by the signs prostrate and do not act arrogantly, reversing the focus ayah's response.
Names the objects worshipped besides God within the same judgment scene.
Its reference to a great matter does not clarify monotheism or arrogant refusal.
Shows a commanded belief being dismissed through a superior, mocking response.
Continues the same tribunal by making the gathered group answerable.
Connects turning away from reminder to God-administered punishment, though it lacks the focus formula.
Explains culpability through refusal to expect accounting, fitting the focus passage's judged rejecters.
Continues the immediate tribunal by exposing the collapse of their mutual support.
The great seizure is not tied to the focus ayah's monotheism or arrogance.
Even those nearest to God do not grow arrogant about worship, directly countering the focus response.
States their compelled submission on the same day of judgment.
Provides the concise declaration of God's oneness that the focus ayah reports being rejected.
Universal prostration to God without arrogance directly contrasts with their arrogant refusal.
Continues the same judgment exchange among those now being questioned.
The great sign does not itself illuminate the rejection of divine oneness.
States the same exclusive divinity formula with God's living, sustaining authority.
Develops the focus passage's tribunal through the followers' accusation against their leaders.
Tests the practical impotence of claimed deities, supporting the focus ayah's rejection of false worship.
States that there is no god but God and grounds that claim in His most beautiful names.
Continues the immediate exchange by locating the followers' own refusal to believe.
Its instruction to speak rightly does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Identifies lack of arrogance as a cause of receptivity, the social and moral opposite of the focus response.
Continues the tribunal by denying that the leaders possessed coercive authority over the followers.
Its small-and-great record concerns scope, not arrogant rejection of monotheism.
States God's exclusive divinity and supreme lordship over the great throne.
Continues the condemned group's recognition that their Lord's word has become binding on them.
A messenger's public declaration offers only a broad parallel to being addressed with divine truth.
Pairs the exclusive-divinity formula with practical reliance on God alone.
Continues the tribunal as the leaders admit they led others astray while astray themselves.
Makes wealth and followers the basis of a spoken claim to superiority, closely matching status-based arrogance.
The victory of God's messengers does not materially clarify this response to monotheism.
States the shared punishment that concludes the same judgment exchange.
Its description of a great struggle does not clarify the focus ayah's refusal.
Shows people replacing what they were told, a related pattern of resisting a divine directive.
Names arrogance, but its immediate concern is malicious plotting rather than response to monotheism.
The severe punishment statement lacks a specific connection to the focus response.
The great signs do not address exclusive worship or arrogant refusal.
Again depicts alteration of what was commanded, but without the focus ayah's central theme.
Links arrogant resistance to God's signs and false claims about Him with humiliating recompense.
Declares God's exclusive divinity and rejects association while naming His true majesty.
Recalling human origin dismantles a boastful self-made claim and thus corrects arrogance.
Depicts resistance when people are told to act in God's path, driven by attachment to worldly life.
A great plot may involve dominating leadership, but it does not directly address the focus response.
Shows hesitation when commanded, though fear and reluctance replace the focus ayah's arrogance.
A prophetic command establishes protected divine claim, but has only a distant relation to the focus.
Its small-and-great expenditures do not clarify monotheism or arrogant rejection.
Explains that worship feels burdensome except to the humble, resonating with the focus reading about resisted obligation.
The oath and punishment passage does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Travel fatigue and a meal request are unrelated to the focus response.
Depicts resistance to God's prior word and attempts to replace it, but not the focus formula or arrogance.
Names arrogance after clear signs and shows that it cannot escape God's eventual judgment.
When told to bow, they refuse, closely paralleling the focus ayah's arrogant response to divine address.
The condemned report calling the warning a great error, a general rejection of divine warning.
Bodily turning away and arrogance in response to an invitation to forgiveness closely mirror the focus response.
Its financial guardianship guidance does not clarify the focus ayah.
When told to stop corruption, they reject the correction and claim the opposite.
The greatness of divine favor does not address exclusive worship or arrogance.
States God's exclusive divinity and reliance on Him alone in the face of turning away.
The disputed damage to the ship is unrelated to the focus ayah.
Exposes speculative excuses for worshipping others besides God, supporting the focus ayah's monotheistic claim.
The great fire does not itself clarify the specific rejection in the focus ayah.
Joins the assertion of one God to hearts that reject it while acting arrogantly.
Addresses an invented claim about God, but lacks the focus ayah's direct refusal of exclusive worship.
Shows that many profess belief in God while still associating partners with Him.
Moses's apology for forgetfulness is unrelated to the focus ayah.
The arrogant acknowledge God's final judgment only after entering punishment.
Condemns saying what one does not do, but does not address monotheism or arrogant refusal.
Describes aversion when God alone is mentioned and delight when others besides Him are invoked, directly paralleling the focus.
Shows a profession of belief that lacks inward reality, a broad but indirect contrast to sincere reception.
Shows a person interpreting worldly favor as personal honor, a limited analogue to status-based pride.
Frames the audience's turning away from a sign as a painful resistance to the messenger's call.
Contrasts making human authorities lords with the command to worship one God alone.
Its warning about large-scale social disorder does not clarify the focus response.
When told to give from God's provision, disbelievers dismiss the command with a deflecting argument.
Defines arrogant earthly self-exaltation through denial of return to God's judgment.
When told to follow revelation, they refuse in favor of inherited practice.
The prophet's call to mindfulness alone does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Iblis's arrogance and refusal of a divine command provide an archetypal parallel to the focus response.
The great success of believers does not clarify the rejection described in the focus ayah.
States the exclusive divinity formula while contrasting God with a materially vulnerable false deity.
Those who deem themselves superior explicitly reject what the vulnerable believers affirm.
When summoned to revelation and the messenger, they refuse and appeal to inherited practice.
The brief prayer for help against corrupters is unrelated to the focus response.
Commands knowledge of the same exclusive-divinity formula and joins it to repentance.
Iblis refuses prostration through arrogance, directly exemplifying refusal before divine command.
The failure to answer the challenge is made evidence that there is no god but God, followed by a call to submit.
States one God and forbids associating anyone in worship, extending the focus declaration into practice.
Persistent grave sin does not specifically clarify monotheism or arrogance.
The messenger's self-description as a clear warner is too general to clarify the focus response.
Its ethical commands about property, justice, and covenant do not materially clarify the focus ayah.
The confession of not praying indicates exclusion from worship, but not the focus ayah's stated refusal.
A false verbal equation is corrected by God's ruling, offering only a general parallel to rejecting revealed distinction.
A late verbal repentance fails when choice has run out, a distant contrast to timely response.
The gathering around Hell supplies the broader judgment outcome for defiant beings.
Names God as Lord of the present people and their ancestors, reinforcing the sole lordship at issue in the focus formula.
The failure to prostrate to the God who knows hidden things sharply contrasts with rightful worship of Him alone.
Defines contested teaching about Jesus by the word of truth, but only indirectly bears on exclusive divinity.
Declares one God and that there is no god except Him, directly supplying the focus formula's doctrinal claim.
When told to fear God, pride drives the person into sin, closely matching arrogant resistance to divine address.
God, the angels, and people of knowledge bear witness that there is no god but Him.
Affirms that there is no god except God in a polemic against false theological claims.
Rejects disdain for worshipping God and warns that the arrogant will be gathered before Him.
Identifies God as Creator and Lord with no deity except Him, then draws the consequence: worship Him.
Pairs the statement that there is no god but Him with the command to follow revelation and turn from idolaters.
Links arrogant rejection of God's signs to lasting punishment.
The prophetic call to worship God alone with no other deity states the core claim rejected in the focus ayah.
The arrogant elite contest the faith affirmed by those they deem weak, clarifying the focus reading about threatened status.
Arrogant chiefs resist the prophet's call by threatening expulsion, showing status-backed rejection of divine guidance.
Those who act arrogantly on earth are turned away from God's signs even when they see them.
Pharaoh voices the exclusive-divinity confession only at the point of destruction, contrasting with a timely receptive response.
Hud's call to worship God with no deity besides Him directly repeats the focus ayah's claim.
Salih's call to worship God with no deity besides Him directly repeats the focus ayah's claim.
Shuayb's call to worship God with no deity besides Him directly repeats the focus ayah's claim.
The messengers confront doubt about the Creator and invite repentance, framing rejection as resistance to a clear divine claim.
God sends the command that there is no deity except Him and calls people to fear Him.
States that God does not love those who act arrogantly.
The universal prophetic message is to worship God and avoid false powers, directly supplying the focus contrast.
Forbids taking two gods and affirms that He is one God, followed by a call to fear Him alone.
Forbids setting another god alongside God, linking association to blame and abandonment.
Describes people turning away in aversion when the Qur'an mentions the Lord alone, a close behavioral parallel to the focus ayah.
God's exclusive lordship over heaven and earth grounds the command to worship Him steadfastly.
God declares that there is no deity except Him and immediately commands worship and remembrance.
Argues that multiple gods would have corrupted the heavens and earth, reinforcing exclusive divinity.
States the shared message to every messenger: there is no god but God, so worship Him.
Depicts disputing about God without knowledge in a proud, deflecting posture.
Noah calls his people to worship God, stating that they have no deity other than Him.
A later messenger gives the same call to worship God with no deity besides Him.
Denies that God has a child or any other god with Him, directly excluding divided divinity.
Affirms that there is no god but God, Lord of the noble throne.
When told to prostrate to the Most Merciful, they refuse and increase in aversion.
They deny God's signs despite inward certainty, acting unjustly and arrogantly.
Affirms that He is God and there is no deity except Him, with all praise and judgment belonging to Him.
Declares that the God of the believers and their interlocutors is one God.
When God's signs are recited, the person turns away arrogantly as though not hearing them.
Warns that associating partners with God is a grave wrong, explaining the content of the rejected monotheistic claim.
Challenges the supposed powers invoked besides God and exposes their lack of authority.
Asks whether any creator besides God provides for creation, then states that there is no deity except Him.
Rejects taking gods besides the Merciful because their intercession and rescue are powerless.
States within the same surah that the audience's God is one.
The immediate preceding verse frames the shared punishment of those treated as criminals.
Immediately explains their reaction: they refuse to leave their gods for a messenger they dismiss as a mad poet.
Questions the worship of objects they themselves carve, exposing the incoherence of false deity worship.
Records astonishment that the messenger has made the many gods into one God, directly paralleling the focus rejection.
Identifies God as Creator of all things and concludes that there is no deity except Him.
Affirms that the Ever-Living has no deity except Him and commands exclusive devotional calling.
The messenger announces that the hearers' God is one and calls them to remain upright toward Him.
Ad arrogantly claim superior strength, an explicit status posture corrected by God's greater power.
Challenges whether any gods besides the Most Merciful were ever prescribed for worship.
Affirms that He alone is God in heaven and on earth, consolidating divine authority.
A person hears God's signs recited and then persists arrogantly as though he had not heard them.
Challenges those who call on others besides God to show what authority or creative share their objects possess.
Forbids setting another deity alongside God and presents the warning as a direct divine summons.
Declares that He is God with no deity except Him and grounds that claim in His knowledge of the unseen and seen.
